title: The tree of life
summary: The tree planted in Eden and barred after the fall stands open again in the middle of the city of God.

stops.note: God plants the tree of life in the middle of the garden alongside the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
After the fall the humans are sent out of Eden and cherubim with a flaming sword guard the way to the tree of life.
Wisdom is called a tree of life to those who take hold of her, keeping the image alive outside the garden story.
Trees on both banks of the temple river bear fresh fruit every month, and their leaves are for healing.
The one who conquers in Ephesus is promised the right to eat from the tree of life in the paradise of God.
The tree of life grows beside the river in the city, yielding twelve kinds of fruit, with leaves for the healing of the nations.
Those who wash their robes are blessed with the right to the tree of life and entry through the gates.

meaning: The tree of life stands for life with God that is unending and unspoiled, first offered in Eden and then withheld after human rebellion. The prophets and wisdom writers keep it alive as a picture of renewal and healing. In Revelation the way back is open again, so the end of the story answers its beginning.
culture: Sacred trees were common in Ancient Near Eastern art, such as the stylised tree flanked by winged figures in Assyrian palace reliefs. Second Temple writers expected the tree to be restored: 1 Enoch 24-25 describes a fragrant tree to be given to the righteous and transplanted near the house of the Lord, and 4 Ezra 8:52 says paradise is opened and the tree of life planted for the faithful. In Ephesus the great temple of Artemis offered asylum within its sacred precinct, and some scholars have suggested that the promise of 'the paradise of God' was heard against that background.
compare: Revelation fuses Genesis and Ezekiel: Eden's single tree and Ezekiel's many riverside trees become one tree, or a row of trees, on both sides of the river. Ezekiel's leaves heal the land, while Revelation's leaves heal 'the nations', widening the scope. The guarded way of Genesis 3 is reversed, since the gates are now never shut.
views: Preterist readers often see the tree as the life of the new covenant now offered in Christ after the old order passed; historicist and futurist readers usually place its full enjoyment in the eternal state after the final judgment; idealist readers take it as a picture of the life with God that believers taste now and receive fully at the end.

title: The river and the water of life
summary: From Eden's river to Ezekiel's temple stream, living water flows until it pours from the throne of God and the Lamb.

stops.note: A river flows out of Eden to water the garden and divides into four rivers.
A river whose streams make glad the city of God flows through the holy dwelling of the Most High.
Everyone who thirsts is invited to come to the waters and receive without money and without price.
The Lord calls himself the fountain of living waters whom his people have forsaken.
Water flows from under the threshold of the temple and deepens into a river that brings life to the Dead Sea.
On the day of the Lord living waters flow out from Jerusalem to the eastern and western seas.
At the feast of Tabernacles Jesus invites the thirsty to come to him and promises rivers of living water.
The one on the throne promises to give water from the spring of the water of life to the thirsty without payment.
The angel shows John the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb.

meaning: Water in a dry land means life, and the Bible uses flowing water as a picture of God himself giving life, cleansing and renewal. The river begins in Eden, becomes a promise attached to the temple and Jerusalem, and is offered personally in the Gospels. In Revelation it flows from the throne, so life comes directly from God and the Lamb.
culture: In Ancient Near Eastern myth gods often dwelt on a mountain at the source of the rivers, as the Canaanite god El did at the source of the two deeps, and temples were linked with springs. In the Second Temple period the feast of Tabernacles included a daily water-pouring ceremony at the altar (Mishnah Sukkah 4:9), the setting for John 7. The cities of Roman Asia prided themselves on aqueducts and ornate public fountains, so a free river flowing through a city carried civic as well as religious meaning.
compare: Revelation draws chiefly on Ezekiel 47 but makes the throne, rather than the temple threshold, the source, because the city has no temple. The invitation of Isaiah 55 to drink without price is repeated almost word for word in Revelation 21:6 and 22:17. Unlike Ezekiel's river, which heals the salt sea, Revelation's river flows in a world where the sea is no more.
views: Preterist and idealist readers often take the river as the life of the Spirit given through the gospel in the present age as well as at its completion; historicist and futurist readers usually locate the vision in the new creation after the final judgment, though many of them also apply the invitation of 22:17 to the present.

title: The sea and the beast from the sea
summary: The restless sea and its monsters, from the deep of Genesis to Leviathan and Daniel's beasts, until the sea is no more.

stops.note: Darkness lies over the face of the deep before God speaks order into creation.
God asks Job whether he can draw out Leviathan with a fishhook, showing the monster is under God's power alone.
God is praised for dividing the sea, breaking the heads of the sea monsters and crushing the heads of Leviathan.
On that day the Lord will punish Leviathan the fleeing and twisting serpent and slay the dragon in the sea.
The four winds stir up the great sea and four great beasts come up out of it, representing successive kingdoms.
Jesus rebukes the wind and says to the sea, 'Peace! Be still!', and there is a great calm.
John sees a beast rising out of the sea with ten horns and seven heads and blasphemous names.
In the new heaven and new earth John notes that the sea was no more.

meaning: In the Bible the sea often stands for chaos, danger and forces hostile to God, though it is never an equal rival: God made it, sets its bounds and tames its monsters. Leviathan and the dragon of the sea become pictures of oppressive powers such as Egypt, and Daniel's beasts from the sea are empires. Revelation gathers these into one beast from the sea and ends with the sea's disappearance.
culture: Babylonian myth told of Marduk defeating Tiamat, the salt-water deep, and Ugaritic texts tell of Baal defeating Yam (Sea) and Litan, 'the twisting serpent, the tyrant with seven heads' (KTU 1.5 I 1-3), wording close to Isaiah 27:1. Jewish writings such as 1 Enoch 60:7-8, 4 Ezra 6:49-52 and 2 Baruch 29:4 speak of Leviathan kept for the end time. For Christians in Roman Asia, Roman governors and power arrived across the Aegean, so a beast rising from the sea could readily suggest Rome.
compare: Revelation combines Daniel's four beasts into one, giving it the leopard, bear and lion features and the ten horns, while its seven heads echo the many-headed Leviathan. Where the Psalms celebrate God's past victory over the sea, Revelation shows the beast's present apparent success and then a final reversal in which the sea itself is removed. Revelation also has a calm 'sea of glass' before the throne (4:6; 15:2), a reminder that the sea is under God's rule.
views: Preterist readers commonly identify the beast from the sea with Rome and often Nero; historicist readers have usually seen it as a long-running power such as papal Rome; futurist readers expect a final individual ruler and empire; idealist readers take it as political power that demands worship in any age. The removal of the sea is read either as the end of chaos and evil generally or as a literal feature of the new creation.

title: The dragon, that ancient serpent
summary: The serpent of Eden, the sea dragon of the prophets and Satan are revealed as one enemy who is thrown down and finally bound.

stops.note: The serpent, more crafty than any other beast, questions God's word to the woman.
God puts enmity between the serpent and the woman, and between their offspring, with a crushing of the head and a bruising of the heel.
God's hand pierced the fleeing serpent, a picture of his mastery over the powers of chaos.
The arm of the Lord is called on as the one who cut Rahab in pieces and pierced the dragon, recalling the Exodus.
Pharaoh king of Egypt is addressed as the great dragon lying in the midst of his streams.
Jesus says he saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven as his disciples carried out their mission.
Paul promises that the God of peace will soon crush Satan under the believers' feet, echoing Genesis 3:15.
The great dragon, the ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, is thrown down to the earth with his angels.
An angel seizes the dragon, that ancient serpent, and binds him for a thousand years.

meaning: The thread joins the deceiver in the garden with the chaos monster of the poets and the oppressive empires the prophets called dragons. Scripture never treats the serpent as God's equal, and from Genesis 3:15 onward it promises his defeat through the woman's offspring. Revelation names the dragon plainly as Satan and shows his defeat in stages.
culture: Ancient Near Eastern myths featured serpent and dragon enemies of the gods, such as Tiamat in Babylon and the serpent Apophis in Egypt. Second Temple writers linked the Eden serpent with the devil, as in Wisdom of Solomon 2:24, 'through the devil's envy death entered the world'. In the Greek world the story of the dragon Python pursuing the pregnant goddess Leto, whose son Apollo later killed it, was well known in Asia, and emperors such as Nero associated themselves with Apollo, so Revelation 12 may deliberately retell a familiar myth with different heroes.
compare: Revelation 12 combines Genesis 3 (serpent, woman, offspring) with the sea dragon of Isaiah and Ezekiel, and gives the dragon the seven heads and ten horns that it then passes to the beast. Unlike the Psalms, where the dragon is already slain, Revelation shows him thrown down yet still raging for a short time. The final stop goes further than any source, with binding, release and final destruction in the lake of fire.
views: Interpreters agree the dragon is Satan; they differ over timing. Many preterist, idealist and amillennial readers see the casting down and binding as achieved through Christ's death and resurrection, so that the gospel goes to the nations, while futurist and premillennial readers usually see the binding of 20:2 as a future event after Christ's return; historicists have linked the stages to periods of church history.

title: The Lamb
summary: From the lamb God provides and the Passover lamb to Isaiah's silent sufferer, the Lamb who was slain stands at the centre of the throne.

stops.note: Abraham tells Isaac that God will provide for himself the lamb for a burnt offering.
Each household takes a lamb without blemish and puts its blood on the doorposts on the night of the Passover.
The servant is led like a lamb to the slaughter and does not open his mouth.
John the Baptist points to Jesus as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.
Paul calls Christ our Passover lamb who has been sacrificed.
Believers are ransomed by the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot.
John hears of the Lion of Judah but sees a Lamb standing as though slain, with seven horns and seven eyes.
The kings make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb conquers them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings.
A great multitude rejoices because the marriage of the Lamb has come and his bride has made herself ready.

meaning: The lamb is the Bible's chief picture of a substitute whose death brings rescue: the provided lamb, the Passover lamb whose blood protects, and the servant who suffers silently for others. The New Testament applies all of these to Jesus. Revelation makes the Lamb its main title for Christ, used about 28 times, and shows the slain Lamb sharing God's throne and worship.
culture: Passover was the great feast of liberation in Second Temple Judaism, with lambs slaughtered at the Jerusalem temple. In 1 Enoch's Animal Apocalypse (1 Enoch 89-90) Israel is pictured as sheep and a horned lamb or ram leads them in battle, showing that a lamb with horns could be a warrior-leader. In the Greco-Roman world sacrificial animals were everywhere, but power was celebrated through the lion, the eagle and the victorious general, so a slaughtered lamb as world ruler challenged every imperial symbol.
compare: Revelation 5:5-6 is a deliberate reversal: John hears 'Lion' but sees a slaughtered Lamb, so messianic conquest is redefined by sacrifice. Revelation uses a different Greek word (arnion) from John's Gospel (amnos) and adds seven horns and seven eyes, combining sacrifice with fullness of power and knowledge. The Lamb is not only a victim but a shepherd (7:17), a warrior (17:14) and a bridegroom (19:7), roles none of the sources combine.
views: All schools of interpretation take the Lamb as Christ crucified and risen, and many describe Revelation 5 as the interpretive centre of the book. They differ chiefly on the timing of the Lamb's war and marriage: preterist and idealist readers often see the victory as won at the cross and worked out in history, while historicist and futurist readers place its decisive completion at Christ's return.

title: The four living creatures
summary: The cherubim who guard Eden and the ark and carry Ezekiel's throne become the four creatures who lead heaven's worship.

stops.note: God places cherubim east of Eden with a flaming sword to guard the way to the tree of life.
Two golden cherubim with outstretched wings overshadow the mercy seat on the ark of the covenant.
Solomon sets two great olivewood cherubim overlaid with gold in the inner sanctuary of the temple.
Six-winged seraphim above the Lord's throne call to one another, 'Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts.'
Ezekiel sees four living creatures, each with four faces of a human, a lion, an ox and an eagle.
Ezekiel recognises that the living creatures under the God of Israel are cherubim.
The cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat are recalled as part of the earthly sanctuary.
Around the throne are four living creatures full of eyes, like a lion, an ox, a man and an eagle, each with six wings, singing 'Holy, holy, holy'.
The four living creatures and the elders fall down and worship God, saying 'Amen. Hallelujah!'

meaning: Cherubim are guardians of God's holy presence and bearers of his throne, marking the boundary between the holy God and his creation. Seraphim add the note of unceasing praise of God's holiness. In Revelation the creatures represent the whole living creation gathered in worship and take part in calling forth the judgments.
culture: Winged composite guardians, such as the Assyrian lamassu at palace gates and Egyptian sphinxes, were common across the Ancient Near East, and a Megiddo ivory shows a king on a throne flanked by winged creatures. Second Temple texts multiply angelic orders around the throne: 1 Enoch 71:7 names seraphim, cherubim and ophanim, and the Dead Sea Scrolls Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice describe cherubim blessing the chariot-throne. From Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.11.8) onward, Christians linked the four faces with the four Gospels, and some modern scholars have compared them with prominent constellations.
compare: Revelation merges Ezekiel and Isaiah: the creatures have Ezekiel's lion, ox, human and eagle and his many eyes, but Isaiah's six wings and Trisagion. Ezekiel gives each creature four faces, whereas Revelation gives each a single face. Their role also grows, since they summon the four horsemen (6:1-7) and hand the bowls of wrath to the angels (15:7).
views: Most interpreters of every school take the creatures as exalted angelic beings representing creation's worship. Some older readers, following the King James wording of Revelation 5:9-10 ('redeemed us'), took them as representing the redeemed, and some historicists linked them with the church or its ministers; idealist readers stress their role as symbols of all creation praising God.

title: Babylon the great
summary: From the tower of Babel to the empire that burned the temple and on to the great city of Revelation, Babylon is the city that exalts itself against God.

stops.note: The city whose builders sought to make a name for themselves is called Babel, because there the Lord confused their language.
The Babylonian army burns the house of the Lord, the king's house and all the houses of Jerusalem.
A watchman announces, 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon,' and her idols lie shattered on the ground.
Babylon is a golden cup that made the nations drunk with her wine, and she has suddenly fallen.
A scroll tied to a stone is thrown into the Euphrates as a sign that Babylon will sink and rise no more.
Nebuchadnezzar boasts of 'great Babylon, which I have built' by his own power and for his own glory.
Peter sends greetings from 'she who is at Babylon', widely taken as a cipher for Rome.
The woman on the beast bears the name 'Babylon the great, mother of prostitutes and of earth's abominations'.
An angel throws a great millstone into the sea, saying Babylon will be thrown down with such violence and found no more.

meaning: Babylon is the archetype of human civilisation organised in pride and rebellion against God: self-made greatness, idolatry, oppression of God's people and seductive wealth. Historical Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and the temple, so the name carried memories of exile. In Revelation it becomes the great city whose luxury and violence are judged, set against the bride, the New Jerusalem.
culture: After Rome destroyed the second temple in AD 70, Jewish writers used 'Babylon' as a code name for Rome, as in 4 Ezra 3:1-2, 2 Baruch 11:1 and Sibylline Oracles 5.143 and 5.159. Rome was famous as the city on seven hills (compare Revelation 17:9), and the goddess Roma was worshipped in temples in Asia, such as the temple of Roma and Augustus at Pergamum, and pictured on coins seated on the seven hills. Revelation 18's cargo list of luxury goods matches the trade flowing into Rome from across the empire.
compare: Revelation 17-18 is built largely from the prophets' oracles against Babylon (Isaiah 13, 21 and 47; Jeremiah 50-51), and also against Tyre (Ezekiel 26-28), whose sea trade lament shapes the merchants' dirge. Jeremiah's stone in the Euphrates becomes a great millstone thrown into the sea. A new feature is the image of Babylon as a prostitute riding the beast, which combines prophetic language for unfaithful cities with a critique of economic power.
views: Preterist readers divide between Babylon as first-century Jerusalem and as imperial Rome; historicist readers have commonly identified it with papal Rome; futurist readers expect either a rebuilt city of Babylon in Iraq or a future world city and system; idealist readers take it as the seductive political and economic order opposed to God in every age.

title: Jerusalem, Zion and the New Jerusalem
summary: David's city of Zion becomes the prophets' jewelled city of hope and finally the holy city coming down from heaven as a bride.

stops.note: David captures the stronghold of Zion, which becomes the city of David.
God promises afflicted Zion foundations of sapphires, gates of jewels and walls of precious stones.
God creates new heavens and a new earth and makes Jerusalem a joy, where weeping will be heard no more.
The restored city has twelve gates named after the tribes, and its name is 'The Lord is there'.
Paul contrasts the present Jerusalem with the Jerusalem above, which is free and is our mother.
Believers have come to Mount Zion, the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem.
The conqueror in Philadelphia is promised the name of the new Jerusalem, which comes down from God out of heaven.
John sees the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.
The city has twelve gates named for the tribes, twelve foundations named for the apostles, and equal length, width and height.

meaning: Jerusalem, or Zion, is the place where God chose to set his name and dwell among his people, and so it becomes a symbol of the whole people of God and of their hope. The prophets promise a restored and beautified city after judgment. The New Testament speaks of a heavenly Jerusalem already reached by faith, and Revelation shows it descending to a renewed earth.
culture: Second Temple writers described a glorious future Jerusalem: Tobit 13:16-17 speaks of gates of sapphire and emerald, 4 Ezra 10 has a mourning woman transformed into a city, and 2 Baruch 4:2-6 describes a heavenly city prepared beforehand. Dead Sea Scrolls fragments known as the New Jerusalem text (for example 4Q554 and 5Q15) describe a vast measured city with gates named after the tribes. Greek cities in Asia were laid out on grids and celebrated their walls and gates, and Herodotus (Histories 1.178) described Babylon as a perfect square.
compare: Revelation draws especially on Isaiah 54, Isaiah 65 and Ezekiel 40-48, but changes key features: Ezekiel's city surrounds a temple, while Revelation's city has none because God and the Lamb are its temple. The city is a cube, like the holy of holies in 1 Kings 6:20, so the whole city becomes the inner sanctuary. The twelve tribes and twelve apostles are joined in one structure, and the city is also a bride, set in contrast with the prostitute Babylon.
views: Futurist readers generally take the New Jerusalem as a real city in the eternal state, some also linking it to the millennium; historicist readers usually place it after the final judgment; preterist readers often see it as the new covenant community established as the old Jerusalem fell, still moving toward completion; idealist readers take it chiefly as a picture of the glorified people of God themselves.

title: The temple and the tabernacle
summary: God's desire to dwell with his people runs from the garden to the tabernacle and temple, through Christ and the church, to a city with no temple.

stops.note: The man and woman hear the Lord God walking in the garden, which many read as the first sanctuary.
God tells Moses to make a sanctuary so that he may dwell among the people, following the pattern shown on the mountain.
At the dedication of Solomon's temple a cloud fills the house and the glory of the Lord fills it.
God promises to set his sanctuary among his people for evermore, saying 'My dwelling place shall be with them'.
The Word became flesh and dwelt, literally pitched his tent, among us, and we saw his glory.
Paul tells the church that they are God's temple and that God's Spirit dwells in them.
John is told to measure the temple of God, the altar and the worshippers, but to leave out the outer court, trampled for forty-two months.
A loud voice announces that the dwelling place of God is with humanity, and he will dwell with them.
John sees no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb.

meaning: The tabernacle and temple are where heaven and earth meet and God's presence lives among his people, guarded by holiness and sacrifice. The New Testament locates that presence in Jesus and then in the Spirit-filled community. Revelation brings the theme to its goal, where God's presence fills the whole new creation and no separate building is needed.
culture: Ancient Near Eastern temples were seen as the dwelling of a god, often modelled as a cosmic mountain or garden with an image of the deity at its centre. At Qumran the community saw itself as a holy house replacing the corrupted Jerusalem temple (1QS 8:5-9), and Jews everywhere felt the loss when Rome burned the temple in AD 70. In Roman Asia cities competed for the title of 'temple warden' (neokoros) of the imperial cult, and Ephesus had both the famous temple of Artemis and a temple to the emperors.
compare: Revelation uses the heavenly temple throughout the visions, with altar, incense and the 'tent of witness' (15:5), as the source of judgment and prayer. Revelation 21:3 echoes Ezekiel 37:27 and Leviticus 26:11-12 but widens 'his people' to 'his peoples' in many manuscripts. The final reversal is that Ezekiel's long temple vision ends in a city with no temple at all, because the whole city is filled with God's glory.
views: The temple of Revelation 11 divides interpreters: many preterists, holding an early date, take it as the Herodian temple before AD 70; futurists commonly expect a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem; historicist and idealist readers usually take it as the church as God's people. On Revelation 21 most agree it describes God's full presence with his people, differing over whether that is wholly future or already begun.

title: The throne and the rainbow
summary: From the covenant bow after the flood to the thrones seen by Isaiah, Ezekiel and Daniel, the throne of God circled by a rainbow is the centre of Revelation's world.

stops.note: God sets his bow in the cloud as the sign of his covenant never again to destroy the earth by flood.
Moses and the elders see the God of Israel, with something like a pavement of sapphire stone under his feet.
Micaiah sees the Lord sitting on his throne with all the host of heaven standing beside him.
The Lord is in his holy temple; his throne is in heaven, and his eyes see the children of mankind.
Isaiah sees the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, with his train filling the temple.
Above the creatures is a sapphire throne with a human-like figure, surrounded by brightness like the bow in the cloud on a day of rain.
Thrones are placed, the Ancient of Days takes his seat on a fiery throne, the court sits and the books are opened.
John sees a throne in heaven with one seated on it like jasper and carnelian, and a rainbow like an emerald around it.
John sees a great white throne and the one seated on it, from whose presence earth and sky flee.

meaning: The throne stands for God's sovereign rule over heaven and earth, and the throne-room visions show that history is governed from there. The rainbow recalls God's covenant mercy after the flood, so his rule is joined with faithfulness to creation. Revelation uses the word 'throne' more than any other New Testament book, and nearly every vision is related to it.
culture: Ancient Near Eastern texts pictured gods enthroned among a divine council, such as El presiding over the assembly at Ugarit. Second Temple visionaries elaborated the throne: 1 Enoch 14:18-22 describes a lofty crystal throne with wheels like the sun and streams of fire, and the Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice from Qumran describe the chariot-throne praised by angels. Scholars such as David Aune have argued that Revelation 4-5 echoes Roman imperial court ceremonial, with acclamations, prostration and the casting down of crowns, so that heaven's court outranks Caesar's.
compare: Revelation 4 combines Ezekiel 1 (throne, creatures, the bow-like radiance), Isaiah 6 (seraphic cry) and Daniel 7 (court, books, a figure who receives authority). Ezekiel's radiance 'like a bow' becomes a full emerald rainbow encircling the throne, and John is more reserved, describing the seated one only in terms of gemstones without a human likeness. Daniel's plural thrones reappear for the elders and for those who reign with Christ (4:4; 20:4).
views: All schools take the throne as God's present heavenly rule. Many dispensational futurists read the call 'Come up here' (4:1) as hinting at the church's removal before the tribulation, while preterist, historicist and idealist readers take Revelation 4-5 as showing heaven's perspective on the whole period that follows. The great white throne of 20:11 is generally read as the final judgment, differing mainly in how it relates to the millennium.
